Gastric feeding had initially been tolerated. A subsequent episode brought increasing vasopressor support, falling urine output, rising lactate, a tender distended abdomen and bloody gastric drainage. Enteral delivery was held while resuscitation and abdominal evaluation proceeded. The following feeding review occurred after that episode.

review.title: Choose local care versus transfer after a scald
fairness: Local wound follow-up with burn-service consultation is the best offered disposition: distinguish the small blistered dermal component from the larger intact erythematous area, then incorporate wound-care tolerance and reliable follow-up. Admission based on the combined visible area is a credible error.

The analgesia and follow-up observations establish a relevant care constraint rather than merely announce outpatient eligibility. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Standalone item; the task is complete when separated from the presentation.
suggestions: Retain the depth-versus-area distinction and concrete wound-care observations. Difficulty is a qualitative prediction, not demonstrated performance. This offline editorial PASS is not source verification or clinical approval.

review.title: Refer a functionally important deep hand burn

cues.phrase: burn surgical service
cues.why: The key repeats the known injury category while the vascular option belongs to a different service and is directly disfavored by the supplied circulation findings. A reader can choose the burn specialist without interpreting depth.

cues.phrase: The fingers remain warm with brisk nail-bed refill and unchanged Doppler signals.
cues.why: Necessary safety information also disposes of the only competing specialist option; the remaining contrast is specialist versus routine dressings.

fairness: Prompt burn-surgical assessment is the best offered plan for this hand/joint injury. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The hand location and restricted finger flexion already justify specialist assessment if the depth descriptions are deleted. Thus the intended depth inference is not consequential in this option set. Standalone and understandable, but below the requested reasoning level.
suggestions: Keep distal perfusion findings. Reframe the decision around a new finding that changes an already plausible burn-service plan, using competing management actions at the same stage rather than a vascular-service foil.
Do not count recognition of a hand burn followed by referral to the burn service as two consequential steps.

review.title: Escalate a changing airway after smoke exposure

cues.phrase: she began pausing between phrases to breathe
cues.why: A lay reader can reject a private car or a later appointment from overt breathing difficulty without interpreting smoke injury or the reassuring saturation.

cues.phrase: Scheduled transfer to the next ambulatory burn appointment
cues.why: An unspecified future appointment is an obviously delayed response beside an emergency transport option.

fairness: EMS transfer is clearly the best offered plan; a normal conventional saturation does not negate the changing airway findings. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
This is an important safety-recognition item, but the choices do not require a second consequential inference. The retrospective setting and task chronology are clear; no earlier node is needed.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as an easy safety-recognition exception, or redesign the scored decision to compare credible stabilization/transport sequences while retaining all airway warning signs.
Remove the explanation's sentence about the founder's clinic setting; it is production framing rather than clinical feedback.

review.title: Match procedural burn care to capability

cues.phrase: it has no monitored procedural-sedation service
cues.why: This directly names the capability supplied by the uniquely different option, 'monitored procedural wound care'.

cues.phrase: after the current oral premedication
cues.why: Both distractors repeat the same unsuccessful approach. The key alone introduces a new treatment capability, allowing novelty-based selection.

fairness: Escalation for monitored procedural wound care is the best offered plan after two incomplete examinations. Small burn size and comfort between procedures do not establish adequate procedural analgesia.

The key is defensible, but the set compares a capability-matched escalation with two repetitions of a failed plan. Interpretation of background versus procedural pain is not needed to defeat those distractors. Standalone chronology is coherent.
suggestions: Preserve the actual failed examination and the clinic's capability boundary. Replace duplicate clinic/home repetitions with distinct, clinically credible next care arrangements.
Avoid naming the key's exact service in the presentation; describe the relevant available monitoring and care resources neutrally, only to the extent needed to distinguish the alternatives.

review.title: Reassess a regionally changing hand burn
fairness: A new burn-surgical assessment is best: worsening central blanching and touch response must be reconciled with less overall pain and epithelialization at the edge, then used to change the existing plan.

Continuing the previously prescribed plan is a credible error. Emergency eschar release is a weaker distractor because no circumferential restriction or distal perfusion deterioration is described, but it does not introduce an alternative defensible key.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The serial exhibit materially changes the decision; this is a standalone case rather than a later node relying on unseen feedback.
suggestions: Preserve the regional trajectory and misleading subjective improvement. If strengthening the third option, use a clinically plausible competing response to the changed wound without removing circulation information.

review.title: Reconcile burn extent and the resuscitation clock
fairness: The supplied worksheet yields 22% dermal-burn TBSA; 3 x 70 x 22 = 4620 mL; half is 2310 mL; subtracting 800 leaves 1510 mL over the remaining four hours, or 377.5 rounded to 378 mL/hour. Exactly one offered answer matches.

693 mL/hour results from including the additional 12% intact erythema; 189 results from spreading the remaining first allocation over eight hours. Both are interpretable errors rather than numerical outliers.

The worksheet explicitly fixes the protocol; the explanation correctly limits the calculation to that worksheet rather than claiming a universal starting coefficient. First node of a coherent fluid sequence; it does not disclose the later response-based adjustment.
suggestions: Retain the explicit local worksheet and rounding instruction. This is burn-resuscitation arithmetic, not a statistics item subject to the single-skill statistics exception.

review.title: Adjust fluids to the acquired response
fairness: Reduce crystalloid with reassessment is the best offered direction: interpret urine output relative to the 70-kg patient and current perfusion, then weigh the improving resuscitation markers against increasing edema.

Stable pressure, falling lactate, patent drainage and the excluded alternative causes of high output make the trend interpretable without inventing an exact rate reduction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The new update is consequential and coherent after the starting-rate calculation. It does not require recalling which numerical answer was previously chosen; current weight, response and task are available in the presentation/update.
suggestions: Retain the direction-only choices and reassessment. Do not turn this into a universal urine-output or percentage-reduction rule.

review.title: Relieve restrictive thermal eschar
clarityIssues: The task asks for a 'decompression plan', but continued elevation is not a decompression procedure. That wording partly filters the choices before the clinical inference.

cues.phrase: Which decompression plan
cues.why: The task selects the procedural category containing escharotomy and fasciotomy while excluding the elevation choice.

cues.phrase: the limb elevated; these findings persisted
cues.why: The third choice, 'Continue forearm elevation', repeats an explicitly unsuccessful action and provides little discrimination.

fairness: Escharotomy with reassessment is the best offered first intervention for persistent local perfusion deterioration beneath circumferential thermal eschar after reversible external compression has been addressed.

Differentiating skin restriction from a deeper compartment problem is a meaningful second step. The explanation appropriately allows deeper decompression when indicated rather than claiming fasciotomy is never needed.

First node of the paired thermal case is coherent and self-contained. Its explanation will prime eschar release in the later chest node, although that node still adds ventilator-mechanics interpretation.
suggestions: Use a neutral complete task such as which immediate intervention is indicated, so every option answers it.

Keep the failed simple measures as safety/sequence data. Replace repeated elevation with a credible alternative at the current stage, or otherwise strengthen the competing mechanism decision without withholding the need for urgent release.

review.title: Recognize restrictive chest eschar
fairness: Thoracic escharotomy is the best offered procedure: simultaneous peak/plateau pressure rise during passive ventilation indicates a compliance problem, and the circumferential chest burn with poor excursion localizes a plausible restrictive cause.

The tube-patency and bilateral pleural findings are relevant checks against the offered alternatives. These are clinical observations requiring interpretation, not a diagnosis label or explanatory option.

The earlier limb-node explanation primes the general eschar-release principle and likely lowers difficulty, but it does not teach the pressure interpretation. The later update supplies its own current findings and can be solved without the earlier answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the passive-ventilation and inspiratory-hold details; they make the pressure comparison fair. Do not rate this as an unprimed hard item when shown immediately after limb escharotomy.
Remove the final explanation sentence about procedures not occurring in the founder's clinic if editing feedback; it adds no clinical reasoning.

review.title: Resuscitate occult electrical muscle injury
clarityIssues: The record gives falling urine output and rising creatinine without quantifying the output or describing current intravascular/volume-overload findings. It does not clearly distinguish inadequate resuscitation from established oliguric renal injury when choosing more fluid.
fairness: Increasing monitored crystalloid is the most plausible intended answer for significant muscle injury on maintenance fluids. I am not asserting it is clinically wrong.

However, rising creatinine and oliguria do not by themselves establish that additional fluid is beneficial. The absence of a volume assessment is a fairness limitation, not a basis for inventing a fluid target.

The first node does not give away the later fasciotomy decision. Its muscle-injury exhibit is coherent with the later compartment complication, but most of the first decision remains a familiar recognition-to-treatment association. The myoglobin result and CK are legitimate clinical data, not a demonstrated wording-only shortcut; the difficulty concern is the lack of a credible competing fluid decision.
suggestions: Supply concise observed fluid balance, urine-output trajectory and cardiopulmonary/perfusion findings sufficient to distinguish under-resuscitation from renal injury with fluid accumulation.
Build the second step around an actual competing fluid decision resolved by those findings, without adding an unsupported exact resuscitation or urine target.

review.title: Release a deep compartment after electrical injury
fairness: Forearm fasciotomy is the best offered procedure: evolving tension, passive-stretch pain and motor change identify a threatened deep compartment, then pliable skin and the electrical mechanism distinguish fascial decompression from eschar release.
Maintained Doppler signals are a useful competing observation and do not make thrombectomy preferable or exclude a compartment emergency. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The previous node establishes muscle injury but does not name the later procedure. The acquired examination changes the decision and contains sufficient current findings to stand alone with the shared presentation.
suggestions: Retain the pulse-versus-compartment distinction and the skin examination. Do not add a pressure cutoff or require a pressure measurement to manufacture difficulty in this clinically overt scenario.

review.title: Investigate reassuring oxygen readings after a fire

cues.phrase: Repeat arterial oxygen tension
cues.why: The stem already reports a high arterial oxygen tension. Repeating the same measurement is a weak foil without a new acquisition or clinical reason.

cues.phrase: Blood co-oximetry
cues.why: The shared 'ox' language with repeated oxygen readings is not sufficient by itself to reveal the key, but the key is also the only novel oxygen-related blood test; the other novel option measures hemoglobin amount.

fairness: Blood co-oximetry is the best offered investigation for suspected CO exposure despite reassuring conventional oxygen measurements. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The task is clear, but it tests the classic fire-plus-reassuring-saturation test association. Rejecting repetition of an already reassuring PaO2 is not a second consequential step.
The initial node is coherent with a later CO severity decision. Its explanation names CO but does not prescribe hyperbaric consultation, so it does not directly give away the later management key.
suggestions: Replace the disposable repeat-test foil with a credible investigation addressing a genuine competing explanation of the patient's observations.

To reach the requested level, test what discordant observed measurements establish and how that changes a concrete next decision; alternatively seek explicit acceptance as foundational CO test recognition.

review.title: Escalate CO care using the clinical trajectory
clarityIssues: The update says she 'still cannot retain three new instructions', but the presentation describes an awake, oriented patient following instructions normally and does not establish an earlier retention deficit. Newly detected impairment, persistent impairment and deterioration are different trajectories.

cues.phrase: Arrange discharge with scheduled neurologic follow-up
cues.why: Discharge is an implausible competitor for a patient unable to retain instructions; it leaves only the meaningful consultation-versus-monitoring comparison.

cues.phrase: without hyperbaric consultation
cues.why: The negative wording defines the second choice as omission of the key's action. This is a legitimate binary clinical comparison but should not masquerade as three equally credible plans.

fairness: Urgent hyperbaric-medicine consultation is the best offered added plan given the pretreatment COHb, documented unconsciousness and cognitive abnormalities. Consultation appropriately avoids claiming universal HBO benefit or mandating treatment from a single number.
The substantive two-step decision is to avoid equating a treated COHb of 4% with resolved clinical severity, then determine whether specialist escalation remains indicated.

The delayed EMS report and pretreatment specimen can fit the sequence. The cognitive chronology needs repair, and the later task must retain its own severe features rather than rely on prior feedback. No confident clinical treatment error identified.
suggestions: State that a formal assessment now detects impaired retention, or document when the deficit began and persisted. Align the explanation's 'persistent cognitive deficits' with that chronology.
Replace the discharge foil with a credible hospital-level competing plan, or present the real consultation decision without padded alternatives. Keep ongoing oxygen and monitoring in shared context.

review.title: Secure a deteriorating smoke-exposed airway

cues.phrase: saliva pools because swallowing is difficult, and inspiratory noise appears
cues.why: The combination makes threatened airway patency unmistakable; waiting during transfer or giving a bronchodilator are not close alternatives.

cues.phrase: Which airway plan
cues.why: 'Secure the airway' in the key closely echoes the task, although the overlap alone is not the main problem. The other choices do not provide comparable airway control.

fairness: Intubation before transfer is clearly the best offered plan. The warning signs must remain; a normal oxygen saturation does not justify waiting. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

This is urgent airway recognition followed by the standard response, with no second consequential decision among credible competitors. It duplicates much of the emergency-disposition item's safety lesson.
The sequence is coherent: later intubation and transfer are consistent with this decision. The first explanation does not explicitly name the later bronchoscopy answer.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as an easy safety item or merge its purpose with the smoke-transfer item. If retaining a routine resident reasoning objective, compare clinically credible airway/stabilization sequences with supported decision-critical observations.
Do not make it harder by removing signs of impending obstruction or adding delay to a clearly indicated airway intervention.

review.title: Investigate lower-airway smoke injury after stabilization

cues.phrase: The burn team needs to assess the distribution and severity of airway mucosal injury.
cues.why: This announces the anatomical target and the rationale for the only direct endoscopic examination, supplying the inference the resident should make.

cues.phrase: The first chest radiograph shows no focal opacity or pleural abnormality.
cues.why: Together with the offered 'Repeat chest radiography', it creates an already-unhelpful-test foil without an interval change justifying repetition.

fairness: Flexible bronchoscopy is the best offered investigation for the stated mucosal assessment after stabilization. CT and radiography have other roles; the explanation does not falsely declare them useless.
The final update sentence fails the teaching-sentence test. Deleting it still leaves enough secretions/pressure findings to ask a neutral next-investigation question.

Chronology after intubation is coherent and the later update supplies a standalone decision. Prior airway feedback primes anatomy but does not directly name bronchoscopy. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Delete the pre-answer statement of the team's mucosal-assessment goal and use a neutral complete next-investigation task.

Replace the repeat-radiograph foil with a credible alternative for the actual unresolved findings. Make stabilization plus interpretation of acquired findings consequential instead of matching a named anatomical target to a scope.

review.title: Choose empiric antidote treatment after a fire
fairness: Immediate hydroxocobalamin is the best offered plan: infer possible cyanide toxicity from the fire exposure, collapse and persistent marked lactate elevation, then account for concurrent CO exposure and hypotension when ranking hydroxocobalamin against nitrite/thiosulfate.

The antidote alternatives are clinically related; awaiting confirmation represents a consequential sequencing error. The send-out assay context is relevant to empiric treatment rather than a generic permission statement.

The explanation appropriately avoids a universal lactate cutoff or an absolute ban on nitrites. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this offline review; comparative antidote evidence and exact clinical sign-off remain for the clinician. Standalone and complete.
suggestions: Retain both the mixed-exposure evidence and the hemodynamic course. Do not turn the constructed lactate value into a diagnostic threshold or imply all smoke exposures require antidote treatment.

review.title: Treat systemic toxicity after an HF burn

cues.phrase: hand spasms on both sides and ventricular ectopy
cues.why: These distant manifestations plus an explicitly low serum calcium make systemic treatment the obvious route; the two localized routes have little remaining plausibility.

cues.phrase: Which calcium treatment route
cues.why: The task supplies the treatment and asks only for its route. Intravenous is the sole systemic option beside two local therapies.

fairness: Intravenous calcium gluconate under monitoring is the best offered route for the described systemic manifestations. Reduced local pain does not establish resolution of systemic toxicity. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Because the low calcium and named treatment are already supplied, the item is principally systemic-versus-local route recognition. The initial local response does not create a difficult second decision once ventricular ectopy and hypocalcemia are given.
Standalone chronology and task are clear. HF systemic toxicity is a worthwhile chemical-burn teaching point, although this review makes no claim about measured exam frequency.
suggestions: Retain the local-versus-systemic distinction and urgent findings. Seek acceptance as focused safety recognition, or test a supported next decision among credible systemic management plans rather than three routes with only one systemic choice.
Do not add unsourced doses, injection concentrations or specialist techniques to manufacture difficulty.

review.title: Apply regional depth to an excision plan
fairness: Planning excision and coverage of the central region is the best offered extent: interpret the repeated central findings alongside the advancing epithelial edge, then avoid applying a whole-wound operative or conservative plan.
The options test a meaningful regional consequence rather than merely naming burn depth. Whole-wound excision and continued dressings are recognizable over- and undertreatment errors.

The central observations support deeper injury but do not distinguish every possible depth with certainty. The wording asks for surgical planning, not an exact operative day or an unconditional claim that all similar wounds require immediate excision.

The first node establishes the operative-field decision without teaching the later donor-limited coverage material. The later operative findings appropriately need to establish bed readiness separately. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the planning wording, serial examination and independently healing peripheral region. Avoid upgrading these observations to an unsupported exact depth or fixed operation deadline.

review.title: Temporize an excised extensive burn

cues.phrase: The team must cover the current bed while those donor regions recover.
cues.why: This states the temporary-coverage rationale before the choice; the key is the only temporary biologic coverage option.

cues.phrase: Reharvest the open donor regions for autograft
cues.why: 'Open donor regions' explicitly advertises why this option is premature, allowing elimination without a real graft-selection decision.

fairness: Cadaveric allograft is the best offered coverage for the prepared extensive bed while autograft donor sites recover. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The viable bleeding bed and donor history are useful observations, but the final update sentence interprets them for the learner. Autograft from still-open donor wounds and topical dressings are weak comparators for the requested extensive coverage.

The later operation follows coherently from excision planning and supplies new bed/donor findings. It stands alone, but its answer follows from the author-supplied coverage goal rather than two consequential inferences.
suggestions: Delete the final interpretive sentence while retaining the actual bed and donor observations.

Replace the overtly premature reharvest option with a clinician-verified competing strategy at the same operative stage, and provide the finding that makes allograft preferable. Do not introduce an unsupported donor-healing timeline.

review.title: Start enteral support after burn resuscitation
fairness: A low-rate gastric enteral start is the best offered plan: infer improving perfusion from the support/lactate/urine trajectory, then distinguish quiet bowel sounds from a reason to withhold enteral nutrition.

Primary PN and waiting for stool represent credible common errors, although the latter is the weaker option. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the item does not claim a universal hour, pressor limit or calorie target.

The first feeding decision is coherent and does not reveal the later deterioration. With the shared presentation, its task is complete. The explanation's perfusion emphasis appropriately scaffolds, but does not answer, the later update.
suggestions: Keep the physiologic trajectory and cautious start. If polishing the presentation, identify the drainage as gastric for precision without adding unnecessary details or cutoffs.

review.title: Pause feeding for a changed burn trajectory

cues.phrase: Urgent resuscitation and abdominal assessment proceed.
cues.why: This preselects the emergency reassessment frame, which the key repeats as 'during reassessment'.

cues.phrase: Pause enteral delivery during reassessment
cues.why: This is the only cautious response to simultaneous worsening shock, a tender distended abdomen and bloody drainage. The two feeding-continuation choices are not close competitors in this overt scenario.

fairness: Pausing enteral delivery is clearly the best offered prescription during this deterioration. A postpyloric tube does not treat compromised bowel perfusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The update genuinely changes the earlier decision and is chronologically coherent, but it piles multiple unmistakable warning signs onto the same conclusion. Recognizing this emergency and stopping feeds is not two consequential steps among credible alternatives.

The first explanation already teaches that perfusion and abdominal findings govern feeding; the later node becomes a straightforward reversal of that rule. Its current findings and task are nevertheless self-contained.
suggestions: Keep all clinically necessary warning signs. Seek explicit acceptance as a safety exception or revise the scored decision to distinguish credible causes of new feeding intolerance using supported acquired observations.
Remove the task-to-key reassessment echo where possible, and avoid retaining two obviously unsafe continuation choices simply to fill the set.

review.title: Interpret a burn surface culture in context
fairness: Continuing the current local regimen is the best offered plan: interpret a surface isolate against objectively improving wound behavior, then decide whether systemic treatment is indicated rather than selecting an antibiotic from susceptibilities.

Ciprofloxacin and cefepime are meaningful temptations because the report names susceptibility, while the wound trajectory and lack of newly described surrounding/systemic illness favor local care. The susceptibility language supports the distractors rather than uniquely cueing the key.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation appropriately calls for reassessment with deterioration rather than claiming a surface culture can never matter. Standalone chronology and task are complete.
suggestions: Retain the clinical trend and the surface-specimen distinction. If revising wording, replace 'surrounding skin are unchanged' with the actual relevant examination so readers need not infer that the previous baseline was benign.

question.stem: Which disposition best fits {patientName}'s scald at this clinic review?

answerChoices.label: Burn-service consultation with local wound follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The dermal component is small, with preserved blanching and manageable wound care. The larger intact erythematous area does not establish a large dermal burn requiring transfer.

answerChoices.label: Burn-service consultation with inpatient burn admission
answerChoices.rationale: Counting every red area as dermal injury exaggerates severity. Current depth, function and care requirements do not establish a need for inpatient admission.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Counting every red area as dermal injury exaggerates severity. Current depth, function and care requirements do not establish a need for inpatient admission.

answerChoices.label: Burn-service consultation with emergency hospital transfer
answerChoices.rationale: There is no physiologic or limb-threatening feature in the recorded course to justify emergency retrieval over planned ambulatory co-management.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: There is no physiologic or limb-threatening feature in the recorded course to justify emergency retrieval over planned ambulatory co-management.

question.explanation: First separate dermal injury from epidermal erythema. Then match the actual wound and care needs to an outpatient pathway. Consultation can help local management; it does not make every scald an inpatient transfer.

caseDefinition.name: Mara Ellis
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 43-year-old woman, attends clinic after a scald to her upper arm and lateral trunk. The wound map records moist pink blistered skin over 2% of body surface and intact red skin over another 12%. The blistered region blanches briskly and remains tender. nodes.displayName: Choose local care versus transfer after a scald

nodes.stem: Which change to {patientName}'s hand-burn plan is supported by the current clinic findings?

options.label: Obtain a new burn-surgical assessment of the wound
options.rationale: Peripheral epithelialization and less pain do not resolve a central region becoming pale, dry and less responsive. The prior plan needs reconsideration.
options.temptation: Interpret central and peripheral regions separately.
options.whenReasonable: This record supports a new assessment; it does not predetermine excision or grafting.

options.label: Continue the existing clinic dressings and exercise schedule

options.whenReasonable: A circumferential deep burn with declining distal perfusion despite appropriate assessment would support emergency eschar release.

nodes.closestError: Continue the old plan because the edge heals, or select escharotomy simply because the center is deeper.
nodes.decidingObservation: Serial central blanching/sensation deteriorate while distal circulation remains preserved.
nodes.counterfactual: If central blanching remained brisk and epithelialization advanced across the center, continuing dressings and therapy would replace repeat surgical depth assessment.

nodes.cueAttack: Complaint and task do not say deepening. The central-versus-edge conflict is required, not rationale paraphrase. nodes.categoryCheck: Three next burn-care plans; no exact graft decision is ranked before specialist assessment.
nodes.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard because lower pain and peripheral healing compete with serial central deterioration.

question.stem: Using the outside hospital's stated worksheet, which starting infusion rate should have been recorded for {patientName} at arrival, rounded to the nearest whole mL/hour?

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 378 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: Count 14% plus 8%, giving 22%. The first allocation is 3 × 70 × 22 / 2 = 2310 mL. Subtract 800 mL, then divide the remaining 1510 mL by the four hours remaining: 377.5 mL/hour.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 693 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result counts the additional epidermal erythema: (3 × 70 × 34 / 2 − 800) / 4 = 692.5. The intact red region does not belong in this dermal-burn estimate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This result counts the additional epidermal erythema: (3 × 70 × 34 / 2 − 800) / 4 = 692.5. The intact red region does not belong in this dermal-burn estimate.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 189 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result restarts an eight-hour window at arrival: (2310 − 800) / 8 = 188.75. The supplied worksheet measures time from the injury.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This result restarts an eight-hour window at arrival: (2310 − 800) / 8 = 188.75. The supplied worksheet measures time from the injury.

question.explanation: The dermal-burn total is 22%, not the 34% of visibly changed skin. The worksheet's first allocation is 2310 mL; 1510 mL remains after transport fluid. Four hours remain in its injury-based window, giving 377.5, rounded to 378 mL/hour. This calculation applies only to the specified worksheet.

reasoningSteps: Interpret the three regional wound descriptions and include partial- and full-thickness regions while excluding intact epidermal erythema.

nodes.closestError: Use the correct clock with all red skin, or the correct burn area with an arrival-based clock.
nodes.decidingObservation: Region C has no dermal injury; four of the eight injury-based hours and 800 mL have already occurred.
nodes.counterfactual: If Region C had dermal injury, 693 becomes the matching worksheet result. If time zero were the injury with a full allocation window remaining, the elapsed-time computation would change.

nodes.categoryCheck: Three starting crystalloid infusion prescriptions under one supplied hospital protocol.
nodes.difficulty: Predicted hard: combines depth-dependent extent with prior fluid and an injury-based clock; arithmetic is exact enough to re-solve without hidden assumptions.
nodes.sequenceCheck: First node. Its explanation gives only this calculation, not the next node's fluid-adjustment answer. Later urine/output observations are not present yet.

nodes.displayName: Adjust fluids to the acquired response
nodes.learningObjective: Reassess the initial burn-fluid prescription using the actual perfusion and urine-output trajectory.
nodes.currentUpdate: Later in the outside admission, the infusion has been increased above its starting rate. Urine output is 90 then 105 mL in consecutive hours. Blood pressure remains stable, lactate is falling, and peripheral edema is increasing. The urinary catheter drains freely; there has been no electrical injury, diuretic administration or hyperglycemic diuresis.
nodes.stem: Which adjustment best fits {patientName}'s later burn-resuscitation record?

options.label: Reduce the crystalloid infusion and reassess the response
options.rationale: The urine/perfusion trajectory and rising edema support reducing an excessive infusion rather than continuing a formula as a fixed obligation.
options.temptation: Use acquired response rather than treating the starting estimate as a quota.
options.whenReasonable: This trajectory supports cautious reduction with continued monitoring.

options.label: Maintain the crystalloid infusion and reassess the response
options.rationale: Maintaining the escalated rate despite high urine output, stable perfusion and accumulating edema risks ongoing over-resuscitation.
options.temptation: Treat the calculated volume as an amount that must be delivered unchanged.
options.whenReasonable: Stable urine output near the treating team's target without edema progression could support maintaining the current rate.

options.label: Increase the crystalloid infusion and reassess the response
options.rationale: There is no current oliguria or worsening perfusion to support further fluid escalation.
options.temptation: Interpret tissue edema as evidence that intravascular replacement must keep increasing.
options.whenReasonable: Persistent low urine output with evidence of inadequate perfusion after checking other causes could support increasing fluid.

nodes.explanation: The response now matters more than the initial arithmetic. High urine output with stable perfusion and increasing edema supports reducing the crystalloid rate with reassessment. This does not teach a universal percentage change or an electrical-injury urine target.
reasoningSteps: Interpret high output, improving lactate and stable blood pressure as a different trajectory from under-resuscitation, while checking important alternative reasons for high output.
Reduce the current infusion to avoid continuing excessive volume delivery.
nodes.closestError: Maintain an escalated rate to satisfy an initial formula despite a changed response.
nodes.decidingObservation: Serial high urine output and improving perfusion coexist with accumulating edema.
nodes.counterfactual: If urine output instead fell with cool extremities and rising lactate, an increase after reassessment would become the relevant fluid direction.
nodes.deletionCheck: The update is necessary: without it none of the three adjustment directions can be ranked. The electrical/diuretic/diuresis information resolves alternative output targets or mechanisms.
nodes.cueAttack: All labels repeat the same reassessment clause; only infusion direction changes. The question does not call the patient over-resuscitated. No unique cautious combined plan supplies the key.
nodes.categoryCheck: Three directions for the same existing infusion at the same time point.
nodes.difficulty: Predicted moderate/hard: over-resuscitation must be inferred despite a large burn and an initially reasonable formula.
nodes.sequenceCheck: The first node establishes only the initial worksheet calculation. This new response is revealed later and changes the decision; preceding feedback does not prescribe reduction.

question.stem: Which decompression plan best fits {patientName}'s right forearm at this point in the outside record?

answerChoices.label: Perform forearm escharotomy and reassess distal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: The regional deterioration under a circumferential deep thermal burn persists despite simple external measures and adequate systemic perfusion, supporting release through constrictive eschar.

answerChoices.label: Perform forearm fasciotomy and reassess distal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: A deeper compartment operation is not the first supported release for this skin-envelope pattern without evidence of muscle injury; reassess after adequate eschar release.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A deeper compartment operation is not the first supported release for this skin-envelope pattern without evidence of muscle injury; reassess after adequate eschar release.

answerChoices.label: Continue forearm elevation and reassess distal perfusion
answerChoices.rationale: The perfusion trajectory worsens despite elevation and removal of external constriction, so continued observation alone does not resolve the mechanical problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The perfusion trajectory worsens despite elevation and removal of external constriction, so continued observation alone does not resolve the mechanical problem.

question.explanation: Local deterioration with stable systemic and opposite-hand perfusion points to the circumferential thermal envelope. Release constrictive eschar, then reassess. Fasciotomy addresses a deeper compartment problem and may be necessary if that problem is demonstrated or perfusion fails to recover after adequate skin release.

caseDefinition.name: Simon Blake
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 52-year-old man, reviews outside burn-unit records with the founder in clinic after recovery. Deep dry burns encircled his right forearm and chest. The first decision below occurred after systemic perfusion had improved during resuscitation.

nodes.displayName: Relieve restrictive thermal eschar
nodes.learningObjective: Distinguish circumferential skin restriction from systemic hypoperfusion and deeper muscle injury when selecting decompression.
nodes.currentUpdate: The right fingers became cooler with slower refill, and palmar Doppler signals weakened on repeated examination. Dressings and jewelry were removed and the limb elevated; these findings persisted. Blood pressure and the opposite hand's perfusion remained unchanged. The arm had no crush or electrical mechanism.
nodes.stem: Which decompression plan best fits {patientName}'s right forearm at this point in the outside record?

options.label: Perform forearm escharotomy and reassess distal perfusion
options.rationale: The regional deterioration under a circumferential deep thermal burn persists despite simple external measures and adequate systemic perfusion, supporting release through constrictive eschar.
options.temptation: Localize the restriction to the burned skin envelope.
options.whenReasonable: This record supports skin release with immediate perfusion reassessment.

options.label: Perform forearm fasciotomy and reassess distal perfusion
options.rationale: A deeper compartment operation is not the first supported release for this skin-envelope pattern without evidence of muscle injury; reassess after adequate eschar release.
options.temptation: Treat all burn-related limb ischemia as a fascial compartment syndrome.
options.whenReasonable: Persisting compartment findings after complete escharotomy or a primary deep muscle-compartment injury could require fasciotomy.

options.label: Continue forearm elevation and reassess distal perfusion
options.rationale: The perfusion trajectory worsens despite elevation and removal of external constriction, so continued observation alone does not resolve the mechanical problem.
options.temptation: Keep a reasonable early edema measure after its documented failure.
options.whenReasonable: Stable perfusion and Doppler findings under surveillance could support elevation without immediate surgical release.

nodes.explanation: Local deterioration with stable systemic and opposite-hand perfusion points to the circumferential thermal envelope. Release constrictive eschar, then reassess. Fasciotomy addresses a deeper compartment problem and may be necessary if that problem is demonstrated or perfusion fails to recover after adequate skin release.
reasoningSteps: Localize the deteriorating perfusion to the burned forearm rather than global hypovolemia or a dressing.
Choose skin-envelope decompression and reassessment before a deeper fascial operation in the stated mechanism.
nodes.closestError: Perform fasciotomy for every ischemic burned limb rather than distinguish the constraining layer.
nodes.decidingObservation: Circumferential deep thermal skin injury with persistent local perfusion decline after dressings/elevation, without a deep-injury mechanism.
nodes.counterfactual: Replace the thermal envelope with high-voltage muscle injury, soft noncircumferential skin and tense painful deep compartments: fasciotomy becomes the relevant release.
nodes.deletionCheck: The opposite limb and systemic trajectory distinguish global perfusion; failed external measures establish escalation; mechanism helps distinguish skin versus muscle. Each changes an offered alternative.
nodes.cueAttack: All options include the same reassessment phrase. The task names no layer. The vignette supplies the necessary restriction and perfusion findings without labelling compartment syndrome.
nodes.categoryCheck: Three decompression/escalation plans for the same threatened extremity.
nodes.difficulty: Predicted hard: the close error is choosing the wrong anatomic release, not ignoring the ischemic hand.
nodes.sequenceCheck: First scored node. Its feedback addresses the forearm and does not pre-teach chest-wall release.

nodes.displayName: Recognize restrictive chest eschar
nodes.learningObjective: Use acquired ventilatory and examination findings to distinguish chest-wall restriction from tube obstruction or pleural disease.
nodes.currentUpdate: Later, during passive controlled ventilation in the outside hospital, delivered tidal volumes fall and both peak and plateau pressures rise; plateau is recorded during an inspiratory hold. A suction catheter passes through the tube and removes little material. Breath sounds are symmetric, bedside pleural ultrasonography shows sliding on both sides, and chest excursion is minimal beneath the circumferential dry chest burn.
nodes.stem: Which immediate procedure best fits {patientName}'s later ventilatory findings in the outside hospital record?

options.label: Thoracic escharotomy
options.rationale: The pressure pattern and restricted excursion localize a compliance problem to the circumferential burned chest wall after the represented tube and pleural checks.
options.temptation: Recognize external thoracic restriction as a reversible cause.
options.whenReasonable: This constructed restriction pattern supports thoracic eschar release.

options.label: Endotracheal tube exchange
options.rationale: An isolated tube obstruction is less consistent with a freely passing catheter and increased plateau as well as peak pressure.
options.temptation: Attribute any abrupt ventilatory difficulty after a fire to an obstructed tube.
options.whenReasonable: A blocked or displaced tube with catheter-passage failure or other tube findings could require exchange.

options.label: Tube thoracostomy
options.rationale: The symmetric examination and represented pleural sliding do not support a pneumothorax as the cause of the marked external restriction.
options.temptation: Treat increased airway pressure as a pleural emergency without integrating the chest examination.
options.whenReasonable: Unilateral loss of sliding with a compatible deteriorating examination would make pleural decompression appropriate.

nodes.explanation: Infer reduced chest compliance from the combined pressures and excursion. Then integrate the tube and pleural checks with the circumferential deep chest wound to select thoracic escharotomy. This is a historical hospital procedure review, not a procedure performed in the founder's clinic.
reasoningSteps: Interpret increased peak and plateau pressure with restricted excursion as a compliance problem rather than simply intraluminal resistance.
Use the wound and represented tube/pleural findings to select release of the chest-wall envelope.
nodes.closestError: Exchange the endotracheal tube for every post-fire pressure rise.
nodes.decidingObservation: Both pressures rise and the chest wall barely moves despite the represented patent-tube and bilateral-pleural observations.
nodes.counterfactual: If the catheter could not pass and plateau pressure remained unchanged, tube obstruction and exchange would become the leading procedure path.
nodes.deletionCheck: Removing the update makes chest release unrankable. Pressure relation, catheter passage and pleural observations each distinguish a specific competing cause; the case header alone is insufficient.
nodes.cueAttack: All options are specific procedures of similar scope. Chest restriction is an observed movement, not an authored diagnosis. Prior forearm feedback does not explain ventilator pressures; the new data must still be interpreted.
nodes.categoryCheck: Three immediate procedures for acquired ventilatory failure.
nodes.difficulty: Predicted hard: external restriction competes with real tube/pleural emergencies and requires integrating several data sources.
nodes.sequenceCheck: Forearm and chest nodes share an injury but test different anatomic consequences. No future respiratory data appear in the first node. Manager should also consider standalone exposure for the chest objective.

question.stem: Which additional blood investigation best addresses {patientName}'s persistent findings after smoke exposure in the initial outside-hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Blood co-oximetry
answerChoices.rationale: COHb can impair oxygen carriage despite a reassuring conventional saturation and high dissolved oxygen tension. Blood co-oximetry directly measures the relevant hemoglobin species.

answerChoices.label: Repeat arterial oxygen tension
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating dissolved oxygen measurement does not establish whether hemoglobin is carrying CO.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating dissolved oxygen measurement does not establish whether hemoglobin is carrying CO.

answerChoices.label: Blood hemoglobin concentration
answerChoices.rationale: Carrier quantity does not measure how much is occupied by CO. It does not resolve this exposure-related discrepancy.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Carrier quantity does not measure how much is occupied by CO. It does not resolve this exposure-related discrepancy.

question.explanation: Separate dissolved oxygen and conventional saturation from functional hemoglobin carriage. A normal reading does not exclude CO exposure. Add blood co-oximetry while emergency clinicians continue appropriate treatment and reassessment.

caseDefinition.name: Tessa Grant
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 41-year-old woman, reviews her outside emergency-hospital records with the founder in clinic. She was removed from an enclosed garage fire and arrived awake and oriented. At the first hospital examination she had persistent headache and nausea but followed instructions normally. Her voice and breathing were unchanged. Finger oxygen saturation was 99%; arterial oxygen tension was high while she received oxygen.

nodes.displayName: Investigate reassuring oxygen readings after a fire
nodes.learningObjective: Recognize what routine oxygen measurements fail to establish after smoke exposure and request blood co-oximetry.
nodes.stem: Which additional blood investigation best addresses {patientName}'s persistent findings after smoke exposure in the initial outside-hospital record?

options.label: Blood co-oximetry
options.rationale: COHb can impair oxygen carriage despite a reassuring conventional saturation and high dissolved oxygen tension. Blood co-oximetry directly measures the relevant hemoglobin species.
options.temptation: Recognize the limits of the existing measurements rather than repeat them.
options.whenReasonable: This exposure and neurologic course justify direct hemoglobin-species measurement.

options.label: Repeat arterial oxygen tension
options.rationale: Repeating dissolved oxygen measurement does not establish whether hemoglobin is carrying CO.
options.temptation: Assume an elevated arterial oxygen tension excludes an oxygen-carriage toxic exposure.
options.whenReasonable: A new oxygenation or ventilation change, or concern about the prior specimen, could justify repeat blood gas assessment.

options.label: Blood hemoglobin concentration
options.rationale: Carrier quantity does not measure how much is occupied by CO. It does not resolve this exposure-related discrepancy.
options.temptation: Investigate oxygen delivery solely through total hemoglobin concentration.
options.whenReasonable: Suspected major blood loss or anemia would make concentration an important separate measurement.

nodes.explanation: Separate dissolved oxygen and conventional saturation from functional hemoglobin carriage. A normal reading does not exclude CO exposure. Add blood co-oximetry while emergency clinicians continue appropriate treatment and reassessment.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the discordance between exposure/neurologic findings and reassuring routine oxygen measurements.
Choose direct hemoglobin-species measurement rather than another measure of dissolved oxygen or carrier quantity.
nodes.closestError: Repeat arterial oxygen tension and treat it as proof that oxygen carriage is adequate.
nodes.decidingObservation: Neurologic findings after enclosed combustion persist despite high measured dissolved oxygen and conventional saturation.
nodes.counterfactual: If the question concerned a new low arterial oxygen tension from a respiratory change, repeat blood-gas oxygen assessment would address that different problem; if low hemoglobin from bleeding were present, concentration would matter.
nodes.deletionCheck: Exposure and symptoms establish the competing oxygen-delivery concern; saturation/oxygen tension establish what has and has not been measured. Stable voice/breathing keeps this at the blood-investigation stage.
nodes.cueAttack: Three named blood measurements have equal placeholder timing profiles. The task does not name CO or request a hemoglobin species. Covered the key: no test alias appears before the options.
nodes.categoryCheck: Three blood investigations addressing oxygen delivery; all are testing choices with exact timing identity/label mappings.
nodes.difficulty: Predicted moderate, with a familiarity risk: the applied measurement-limit distinction is clinically consequential, but independent review should challenge whether PGY-2/3 discrimination is sufficient.
nodes.sequenceCheck: First node. Its feedback does not discuss HBO indications, persistent neurologic findings after oxygen, or the later result.

nodes.displayName: Escalate CO care using the clinical trajectory
nodes.learningObjective: Avoid dismissing severe CO exposure on the basis of a low post-oxygen COHb and select hyperbaric consultation.
nodes.currentUpdate: A pre-treatment specimen later returned with COHb 28%. After high-concentration oxygen, COHb is 4%. She now maintains her airway but still cannot retain three new instructions and repeatedly loses her place during a simple task. An EMS report retrieved after the first laboratory review documents loss of consciousness before arrival. The hospital continues oxygen and neurologic monitoring.
nodes.stem: Which additional care plan best fits {patientName}'s later outside-hospital assessment?

options.label: Seek urgent hyperbaric-medicine consultation
options.rationale: The newly documented loss of consciousness and acquired neurologic deficits remain important despite a lower COHb after treatment. Consultation should consider HBO in the complete clinical setting.
options.temptation: Judge escalation from clinical severity and trajectory, not one treated laboratory value.
options.whenReasonable: This record supports consultation; the specialist team decides treatment and transport suitability.

options.label: Continue monitored hospital care without hyperbaric consultation
options.rationale: Monitored oxygen is already shared background care. With these neurologic features, omitting specialist consideration on the basis of the low treated level underestimates severity.
options.temptation: Use the post-oxygen COHb to make the existing hospital plan sufficient.
options.whenReasonable: A mild exposure with complete symptom resolution and no severe clinical features might be managed without HBO after appropriate assessment.

options.label: Arrange discharge with scheduled neurologic follow-up
options.rationale: Persistent deficits and documented loss of consciousness do not fit a routine discharge decision at this assessment.
options.temptation: Equate biochemical improvement with complete neurologic recovery.

question.stem: Which airway plan best fits {patientName}'s changing findings before the outside-hospital transfer?

answerChoices.label: Secure the airway by endotracheal intubation before transfer
answerChoices.rationale: Progressive voice, secretion and inspiratory changes indicate a threatened upper airway despite preserved saturation; diagnostic work should not delay airway control.

answerChoices.label: Give nebulized bronchodilator treatment before transfer
answerChoices.rationale: The progressive voice and secretion changes with inspiratory noise indicate an upper-airway threat; a lower-airway bronchodilator does not secure that airway.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The progressive voice and secretion changes with inspiratory noise indicate an upper-airway threat; a lower-airway bronchodilator does not secure that airway.

answerChoices.label: Continue oxygen and reassess the airway during transfer
answerChoices.rationale: Oxygen and a reassuring saturation do not prevent mechanical airway obstruction from progressing en route.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Oxygen and a reassuring saturation do not prevent mechanical airway obstruction from progressing en route.

question.explanation: The serial findings concern upper-airway patency, not simply oxygen delivery. Secure that airway before transfer rather than wait for hypoxemia or rely on a lower-airway bronchodilator. Facial soot by itself would not establish this same indication.

caseDefinition.name: Daniel Frost
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 58-year-old man, reviews his outside hospital admission with the founder in clinic after an enclosed workshop fire. At the first recorded assessment he had soot around his mouth and could speak in full sentences. The hospital then documented the serial observations below.

nodes.displayName: Secure a deteriorating smoke-exposed airway
nodes.learningObjective: Interpret an evolving upper-airway trajectory and choose airway control rather than bronchodilator treatment or oxygen observation before transfer.
nodes.currentUpdate: His voice becomes faint and coarse, saliva pools because swallowing is difficult, and inspiratory noise appears. He remains awake and finger oxygen saturation is 97% on oxygen. The outside team is preparing transfer to a burn unit.
nodes.stem: Which airway plan best fits {patientName}'s changing findings before the outside-hospital transfer?

options.label: Secure the airway by endotracheal intubation before transfer
options.rationale: Progressive voice, secretion and inspiratory changes indicate a threatened upper airway despite preserved saturation; diagnostic work should not delay airway control.
options.temptation: Use progression rather than waiting for oxygen desaturation.
options.whenReasonable: This evolving obstruction pattern supports airway control by the outside emergency/anesthesia team.

options.label: Give nebulized bronchodilator treatment before transfer
options.rationale: The progressive voice and secretion changes with inspiratory noise indicate an upper-airway threat; a lower-airway bronchodilator does not secure that airway.
options.temptation: Treat noisy breathing after smoke as lower-airway bronchospasm rather than localize the evolving obstruction.
options.whenReasonable: Predominantly expiratory wheeze with stable voice, secretion handling and no upper-airway progression could support bronchodilator treatment.

options.rationale: Oxygen and a reassuring saturation do not prevent mechanical airway obstruction from progressing en route.

nodes.displayName: Investigate lower-airway smoke injury after stabilization

The burn team needs to assess the distribution and severity of airway mucosal injury.
nodes.stem: Which investigation best addresses {patientName}'s lower-airway assessment in the later burn-unit record?

options.label: Flexible bronchoscopy
options.rationale: Direct examination can establish and grade lower-airway mucosal injury and assess retained airway debris after stabilization.
options.temptation: Recognize that a normal early radiograph does not answer a mucosal-injury question.
options.whenReasonable: This record supports direct lower-airway examination.

options.label: Chest computed tomography
options.rationale: CT can assess thoracic and parenchymal disease, but the specified unresolved question is mucosal distribution and debris within the airway.
options.temptation: Escalate from a normal radiograph to cross-sectional imaging for every unconfirmed inhalation injury.
options.whenReasonable: A concern for occult thoracic trauma or another structural pulmonary process could make chest CT appropriate.

options.label: Repeat chest radiography
options.rationale: A later radiograph can track pulmonary changes but does not directly grade the airway surface or inspect retained debris.
options.temptation: Wait for the initial normal imaging test to become diagnostic.
options.whenReasonable: A new parenchymal or pleural finding or monitoring question could justify repeat radiography.

nodes.explanation: Match the unresolved anatomy to the investigation. After stabilization, direct lower-airway examination can assess the mucosa and debris even when an early chest radiograph is unrevealing. Imaging still has other roles; the key does not declare CT or radiographs useless.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the secretion/pressure course as an unresolved lower-airway problem not excluded by the radiograph.
Choose the modality that directly examines the anatomic target and its severity.

nodes.decidingObservation: Persistent airway particulate material and mechanics changes coexist with a radiograph that does not inspect the mucosal target.
nodes.counterfactual: If the unresolved target were an occult thoracic injury after a blast rather than airway mucosal injury, CT would become the appropriate next modality.
nodes.deletionCheck: The later stable state permits investigation; secretions/pressure establish the unresolved problem; the imaging result distinguishes what is already assessed. Without this update the earlier unstable patient needs stabilization, not this workup decision.

question.stem: Which antidote plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded hospital condition while supportive treatment continues?

answerChoices.label: Administer intravenous hydroxocobalamin now
answerChoices.rationale: The exposure, coma/collapse and profound persistent lactate support empiric treatment for suspected cyanide toxicity. Hydroxocobalamin avoids adding the nitrite-associated methemoglobin burden to documented CO exposure.

answerChoices.label: Administer sodium nitrite with thiosulfate now
answerChoices.rationale: This is a genuine cyanide regimen, but sodium nitrite can worsen hypotension and oxygen carriage through methemoglobin formation when CO poisoning coexists. The preferred available alternative here is hydroxocobalamin.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a genuine cyanide regimen, but sodium nitrite can worsen hypotension and oxygen carriage through methemoglobin formation when CO poisoning coexists. The preferred available alternative here is hydroxocobalamin.

answerChoices.label: Await the blood cyanide result before antidote treatment
answerChoices.rationale: A reference-laboratory result should not defer treatment when severe exposure and clinical findings make suspicion high.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A reference-laboratory result should not defer treatment when severe exposure and clinical findings make suspicion high.

question.explanation: Infer possible cyanide toxicity in addition to the measured CO exposure, then account for the oxygen-carriage and hypotension risks of sodium nitrite when choosing treatment. The history and collapse justify empiric hydroxocobalamin without waiting for a send-out result. Lactate here is a constructed observation, not a universal diagnostic cutoff.

caseDefinition.name: Iris Lane
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 34-year-old woman, reviews her outside hospital records in clinic after an enclosed upholstered-furniture fire. She had soot in her mouth, lost consciousness and arrived with circulatory collapse. Her airway was secured and she received oxygen and circulatory support. Lactate remained 16 mmol/L, and blood co-oximetry showed COHb 19%. The hospital laboratory sent a cyanide assay to a reference laboratory.

question.stem: Which calcium treatment route best fits {patientName}'s later findings in the outside-hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous calcium gluconate
answerChoices.rationale: Bilateral neuromuscular findings, ECG changes and falling serum calcium indicate systemic toxicity; intravenous replacement with surveillance addresses the systemic deficit.

answerChoices.label: Topical calcium gluconate

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Topical treatment targets the exposed skin, but local improvement does not correct the documented systemic calcium deficit and cardiac manifestations.

answerChoices.label: Local calcium gluconate infiltration
answerChoices.rationale: Local infiltration may be considered for selected persistent local injury, but it does not replace systemic treatment for this acquired multisystem pattern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local infiltration may be considered for selected persistent local injury, but it does not replace systemic treatment for this acquired multisystem pattern.

question.explanation: Reduced local pain is not proof that absorbed fluoride is harmless. Interpret the distant spasms, ECG course and serum calcium together, then use the systemic route under monitoring. No injection concentration, dose or intra-arterial technique is prescribed in this draft.

caseDefinition.name: Marcus Vale
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 49-year-old man, reviews his outside hospital record in clinic after concentrated hydrofluoric acid spilled over his forearm. Irrigation and topical calcium treatment had reduced local pain. During monitored hospital observation he developed hand spasms on both sides and ventricular ectopy; the ECG report described a lengthening QT interval. Serum calcium had fallen below the laboratory reference interval.

question.stem: Which regional wound plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded trunk examination when planning burn excision and coverage?

answerChoices.label: Plan excision and coverage of the central region

question.stem: Which initial nutrition plan best fits {patientName}'s first outside burn-unit assessment?

answerChoices.label: Start low-rate gastric enteral nutrition
answerChoices.rationale: The acquired perfusion and abdominal record supports a cautious enteral start. Quiet bowel sounds alone do not establish bowel ischemia or obstruction.

answerChoices.rationale: The record supplies no established reason that the gut route is unusable; a quiet examination alone does not make PN the preferred initial route.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The record supplies no established reason that the gut route is unusable; a quiet examination alone does not make PN the preferred initial route.

answerChoices.rationale: Waiting for stool adds a prerequisite not supported by the represented perfusion recovery and abdominal findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Waiting for stool adds a prerequisite not supported by the represented perfusion recovery and abdominal findings.

question.explanation: Interpret the current resuscitation trajectory and abdominal findings together. They support a cautious enteral start despite quiet bowel sounds. This question does not prescribe an exact hour, calorie target, access procedure or advancement schedule.

caseDefinition.name: Avery Stone
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 46-year-old woman, reviews her outside burn-unit nutrition records with the founder in clinic. Extensive burns required intubation. During the initial feeding review, blood pressure was maintained after vasopressor discontinuation, lactate was falling and urine output was recovering. Her abdomen was soft with nonbloody drainage but quiet bowel sounds. She could not eat while intubated.

nodes.stem: Which initial nutrition plan best fits {patientName}'s first outside burn-unit assessment?

options.label: Start low-rate gastric enteral nutrition
options.rationale: The acquired perfusion and abdominal record supports a cautious enteral start. Quiet bowel sounds alone do not establish bowel ischemia or obstruction.
options.temptation: Integrate the current perfusion trajectory rather than postpone nutrition for a motility sound.
options.whenReasonable: This represented state supports a cautious monitored start rather than immediate full delivery.

options.label: Start primary parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: The record supplies no established reason that the gut route is unusable; a quiet examination alone does not make PN the preferred initial route.

options.whenReasonable: A sustained inability to use the gut can require a separate PN plan after full nutritional assessment.

options.rationale: Waiting for stool adds a prerequisite not supported by the represented perfusion recovery and abdominal findings.

options.whenReasonable: Suspected obstruction or bowel ischemia would require reassessment rather than this automatic early-enteral pathway.

nodes.deletionCheck: Perfusion observations determine current eligibility, the abdomen addresses a competing safety concern, quiet sounds test the misconception, and intubation explains inability to eat. No exact resuscitation cutoff is invented.

nodes.categoryCheck: Three initial nutrition prescriptions at the same care phase.

nodes.displayName: Pause feeding for a changed burn trajectory

question.stem: Which antimicrobial plan best fits {patientName}'s wound at this clinic review?

answerChoices.label: Continue the current antimicrobial dressing regimen
answerChoices.rationale: The healing trajectory and unchanged surrounding skin do not establish infection requiring systemic treatment. Interpret surface growth with the examination and continue reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Add oral ciprofloxacin to the dressing regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Susceptibility states what might treat the organism if systemic therapy were indicated; it does not itself establish that this improving wound requires an antibiotic course.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Susceptibility states what might treat the organism if systemic therapy were indicated; it does not itself establish that this improving wound requires an antibiotic course.

answerChoices.label: Add intravenous cefepime to the dressing regimen
answerChoices.rationale: A susceptible surface organism does not establish deep invasive disease or a need for intravenous therapy in this healing, clinically well patient.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A susceptible surface organism does not establish deep invasive disease or a need for intravenous therapy in this healing, clinically well patient.

question.explanation: First interpret the surface specimen alongside actual wound behavior. Then decide whether systemic therapy is indicated. Healing and an unchanged surrounding examination favor local care; a susceptibility report is not a prescription by itself. New tissue deterioration, spreading inflammation or systemic illness would require reassessment.

caseDefinition.name: Mina Hart
caseDefinition.presentation: {patientName}, a 39-year-old woman, attends clinic for a forearm burn managed with antimicrobial dressings. At consecutive visits the open area has become smaller with new epithelium and less dressing pain. A surface swab taken at the earlier dressing change now reports Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptible to ciprofloxacin and cefepime. The wound margin and surrounding skin are unchanged, and she feels well.

questions.stem: Which disposition best fits {patientName}'s scald at this clinic review?

answerChoices.label: Burn-service consultation with local wound follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The dermal component is small, with preserved blanching and manageable wound care. The larger intact erythematous area does not establish a large dermal burn requiring transfer.

answerChoices.label: Burn-service consultation with inpatient burn admission
answerChoices.rationale: Counting every red area as dermal injury exaggerates severity. Current depth, function and care requirements do not establish a need for inpatient admission.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Counting every red area as dermal injury exaggerates severity. Current depth, function and care requirements do not establish a need for inpatient admission.

answerChoices.label: Burn-service consultation with emergency hospital transfer
answerChoices.rationale: There is no physiologic or limb-threatening feature in the recorded course to justify emergency retrieval over planned ambulatory co-management.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: There is no physiologic or limb-threatening feature in the recorded course to justify emergency retrieval over planned ambulatory co-management.

questions.explanation: First separate dermal injury from epidermal erythema. Then match the actual wound and care needs to an outpatient pathway. Consultation can help local management; it does not make every scald an inpatient transfer.

questions.stem: Which referral plan best fits {patientName}'s hand examination at this clinic visit?

answerChoices.label: Arrange prompt assessment by the burn surgical service
answerChoices.rationale: The depth pattern and joint involvement need specialist planning even though distal circulation is maintained.

answerChoices.label: Arrange continued dressings through the general clinic
answerChoices.rationale: A small surface area does not remove the functional and depth concern over hand joints.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A small surface area does not remove the functional and depth concern over hand joints.

answerChoices.label: Arrange emergency assessment by the vascular surgical service
answerChoices.rationale: Reduced wound sensation can reflect depth; the recorded distal perfusion does not support an arterial emergency as the primary referral target.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reduced wound sensation can reflect depth; the recorded distal perfusion does not support an arterial emergency as the primary referral target.

questions.explanation: Infer a deeper dermal injury from the regional wound findings, then apply the hand/joint consequence. Preserved distal circulation does not make the burn shallow, but it separates this specialist referral from a current constrictive perfusion emergency.

questions.stem: Which transfer plan was appropriate when {patientName}'s voice and breathing changed in the outside urgent-care record?

answerChoices.label: EMS transfer to emergency care with burn-team coordination
answerChoices.rationale: The progressive voice and breathing changes require airway-capable emergency care; normal pulse saturation does not remove that risk.

answerChoices.label: Private-car transfer to a same-day burn-clinic assessment
answerChoices.rationale: A same-day specialist destination does not provide monitored stabilization during an evolving airway problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A same-day specialist destination does not provide monitored stabilization during an evolving airway problem.

answerChoices.label: Scheduled transfer to the next ambulatory burn appointment
answerChoices.rationale: A future wound appointment does not address progressive breathing abnormalities at the recorded visit.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A future wound appointment does not address progressive breathing abnormalities at the recorded visit.

questions.explanation: Interpret the changing voice and breathing as an evolving airway risk, then choose a transport pathway that can provide emergency stabilization. The founder is reviewing a past outside visit; the clinic is not being represented as an emergency department.

questions.stem: Which care arrangement best fits {patientName}'s next wound examination and dressing change?

answerChoices.label: Burn-service assessment for monitored procedural wound care
answerChoices.rationale: Resting comfort does not establish tolerance of the procedure. Repeated incomplete dressing care exceeds this clinic's analgesia and monitoring capability.

answerChoices.label: Clinic dressing changes after the current oral premedication
answerChoices.rationale: The same plan has twice prevented completion of examination and dressing care.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The same plan has twice prevented completion of examination and dressing care.

answerChoices.label: Home dressing changes after the current oral premedication
answerChoices.rationale: Moving the incompletely tolerated procedure home does not supply the missing procedural support or complete the wound assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Moving the incompletely tolerated procedure home does not supply the missing procedural support or complete the wound assessment.

questions.explanation: Separate background comfort from the actual procedure attempted. The failed dressing removals leave wound assessment incomplete; the next care setting must meet that procedural requirement. Burn size alone does not establish outpatient capability.

questions.stem: Which change to {patientName}'s hand-burn plan is supported by the current clinic findings?

answerChoices.label: Obtain a new burn-surgical assessment of the wound
answerChoices.rationale: Peripheral epithelialization and less pain do not resolve a central region becoming pale, dry and less responsive. The prior plan needs reconsideration.

answerChoices.label: Continue the existing clinic dressings and exercise schedule
answerChoices.rationale: The healing edge does not establish recovery of the changed central region across important joints.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The healing edge does not establish recovery of the changed central region across important joints.

answerChoices.label: Arrange emergency release of circumferential burn eschar
answerChoices.rationale: A depth change is not itself a restrictive circumferential perfusion problem. The described dorsal injury and preserved distal findings do not establish that operative indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A depth change is not itself a restrictive circumferential perfusion problem. The described dorsal injury and preserved distal findings do not establish that operative indication.

questions.explanation: Read each wound region and its trajectory. The center's loss of blanching and touch response can represent worsening depth despite a healing edge. Reconsult the burn surgical service for the changed hand injury. Escharotomy addresses mechanical restriction, not depth alone.

questions.stem: Using the outside hospital's stated worksheet, which starting infusion rate should have been recorded for {patientName} at arrival, rounded to the nearest whole mL/hour?

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 378 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: Count 14% plus 8%, giving 22%. The first allocation is 3 × 70 × 22 / 2 = 2310 mL. Subtract 800 mL, then divide the remaining 1510 mL by the four hours remaining: 377.5 mL/hour.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 693 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result counts the additional epidermal erythema: (3 × 70 × 34 / 2 − 800) / 4 = 692.5. The intact red region does not belong in this dermal-burn estimate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This result counts the additional epidermal erythema: (3 × 70 × 34 / 2 − 800) / 4 = 692.5. The intact red region does not belong in this dermal-burn estimate.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 189 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result restarts an eight-hour window at arrival: (2310 − 800) / 8 = 188.75. The supplied worksheet measures time from the injury.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This result restarts an eight-hour window at arrival: (2310 − 800) / 8 = 188.75. The supplied worksheet measures time from the injury.

questions.explanation: The dermal-burn total is 22%, not the 34% of visibly changed skin. The worksheet's first allocation is 2310 mL; 1510 mL remains after transport fluid. Four hours remain in its injury-based window, giving 377.5, rounded to 378 mL/hour. This calculation applies only to the specified worksheet.
